metadata.scope: e_lingnan (177 baronies across k_lingnan, k_lingxi, k_viet)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_dianbai.first_mention_attestation: Established as Dianbai Commandery (电白郡) in 535 CE (Liang Datong 1) and reorganized as Dianbai County in 589 CE (Sui Kaihuang 9).
b_dianbai.etymology_analysis: Classical Chinese toponym combining diàn ('lightning') and bái ('white'), traditionally explained by frequent summer lightning and white clouds/smoke in the coastal hills of western Guangdong; first attested as Dianbai Commandery in 535 CE.

b_maoming.first_mention_attestation: Established as Maoming County (茂名县) in 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18), named after the Jin-dynasty Daoist physician Pan Maoming (b. 290 CE).
b_maoming.etymology_analysis: Eponymous county name established in 598 CE after the Jin-era Daoist alchemist and healer Pan Maoming (潘茂名, c. 290–371 CE); in 634 CE his surname was also given to Panzhou (潘州).

b_baoning.first_mention_attestation: Bao'an County was renamed Baoning County (保宁县) in 757 CE (Tang Zhide 2) under Gaozhou (also recorded under 742 CE Tianbao 1 in local gazetteers).
b_baoning.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang administrative renaming ('protecting tranquility') applied in 757 CE to the earlier Bao'an County (保安县, established 717 CE).

historical_names.name: Bao'an
historical_names.source: Tang Kaiyuan 5 (717 CE) establishment of Bao'an County under Gaozhou
historical_names.notes: Bao'an County was renamed Baoning County during the Tang dynasty (742 or 757 CE).

b_haikang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Haikang County (海康县) in 589 CE (Sui Kaihuang 9) on the Leizhou Peninsula.
b_haikang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious coastal county name ('peaceful sea') created in 589 CE during the Sui dynasty, referring to the county's position bordering the sea on the west and south.

historical_names.name: Xuwen
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Hanshu, Dilizhi; Han Yuanding 6, 111 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Haikang was carved out of Han-era Xuwen County territory on the Leizhou Peninsula.

b_xuwen.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xuwen County (徐闻县) in 111 BCE (Han Yuanding 6) under Hepu Commandery, attested in the Book of Han (Hanshu Dilizhi, 2 CE).
b_xuwen.etymology_analysis: Han-era county name (111 BCE) at the southern tip of the Leizhou Peninsula; traditionally glossed as 'its fame/virtue is gradually heard' or as a sinicized transcription of a local Kra-Dai/Yue toponym.

b_suixi.first_mention_attestation: Tiepa County was renamed Suixi County (遂溪县) in 743 CE (Tang Tianbao 2) under Haikang Commandery (Leizhou).
b_suixi.etymology_analysis: Tang-era auspicious renaming of Tiepa County in 743 CE, meaning 'the converging streams fulfill the people's benefit' (溪水合流，民利遂之).

historical_names.name: Tiepa
historical_names.source: Tang Wude 4 (621 CE) establishment of Tiepa County under Nanhezhou
historical_names.notes: Tiepa County was renamed Suixi County in 743 CE.

b_lianjiang_1.first_mention_attestation: Shicheng County was renamed Lianjiang County (廉江县) on May 9, 1914 CE to avoid duplication with Shicheng County in Jiangxi.
b_lianjiang_1.etymology_analysis: Named in 1914 CE after the Lianjiang River (廉江) flowing through the county, replacing the Tang-era name Shicheng (石城).

historical_names.name: Shicheng
historical_names.source: Tang Wude 5 (622 CE) establishment of Shicheng County under Luozhou
historical_names.notes: Shicheng County was established in 622 CE and became the seat of Luozhou in 623 CE.

b_shilong.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Shilong County (石龙县) under Gaoliang Commandery in 607 CE (Sui Daye 3, Book of Sui), and seat of Luozhou in 622 CE (Tang Wude 5).
b_shilong.etymology_analysis: Toponym combining shí ('stone') and lóng ('dragon'), attested as Shilong County by 607 CE (modern Huazhou, Guangdong).

historical_names.name: Luozhou
historical_names.source: Liu Song Yuanjia 3 (426 CE) establishment of Luozhou County; Southern Qi Gaoxing Commandery
historical_names.notes: Modern Huazhou was previously the seat of Southern Qi Gaoxing County and Liu Song Luozhou County.

historical_names.name: Gaoxing
historical_names.source: Liu Song Yuanjia 3 (426 CE) establishment of Luozhou County; Southern Qi Gaoxing Commandery
historical_names.notes: Modern Huazhou was previously the seat of Southern Qi Gaoxing County and Liu Song Luozhou County.

b_wuchuan_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wuchuan County (吴川县) in 589 CE (Sui Kaihuang 9) under Luozhou.
b_wuchuan_1.etymology_analysis: Sui-era county name established in 589 CE, combining Wú (traditionally linked to a local surname or river name) and chuān ('stream/river').

b_linglu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Linglu County (零绿县) in 622 CE (Tang Wude 5) under Luozhou.
b_linglu.etymology_analysis: Early Tang county name established in 622 CE in western Guangdong (modern Lianjiang area), recorded in the New Book of Tang under Luozhou.

b_haiyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Haiyang County (海阳县) in 331 CE (Eastern Jin Xianhe 6; or 413 CE Yixi 9) when Jieyang County was divided.
b_haiyang.etymology_analysis: Classical Chinese locator compound meaning 'north (sunny side) of the sea', established in the Eastern Jin dynasty (331 CE) as the seat of Yi'an Commandery and later Chaozhou.

historical_names.name: Jieyang
historical_names.source: Qin Shi Huang 33 (214 BCE) Jieyang Garrison; Han Yuanding 6 (111 BCE) Jieyang County
historical_names.notes: Haiyang was split off from ancient Jieyang County in 331 CE.

b_chaoyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Chaoyang County (潮阳县) in 331 CE (Eastern Jin Xianhe 6; or 413 CE Yixi 9) under Dongguan/Yi'an Commandery.
b_chaoyang.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'north of the tidal waters/sea' (海之北，潮汐所及之阳), established in the Eastern Jin dynasty (331 CE).

historical_names.name: Jieyang
historical_names.source: Qin Shi Huang 33 (214 BCE) Jieyang Garrison
historical_names.notes: Chaoyang was split off from ancient Jieyang County in 331 CE.

b_jieyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jieyang Garrison (揭阳戍) in 214 BCE (Qin Shi Huang 33) and Jieyang County in 111 BCE (Han Yuanding 6, attested in Hanshu Dilizhi 2 CE).
b_jieyang.etymology_analysis: Locator compound meaning 'south of Mount Jie / Jieling' (揭岭之南), attested from the Qin conquest of Lingnan in 214 BCE.

b_wanchuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yizhao County (义招县) in 413 CE (Eastern Jin Yixi 9) under Yi'an Commandery; renamed Wanchuan (万川) in 607 CE (Sui Daye 3).
b_wanchuan.etymology_analysis: Eastern Jin county name ('summoning with righteousness') established in 413 CE; renamed Wanchuan ('ten thousand streams') under the Sui in 607 CE before being merged into Haiyang in the early Tang.

b_haining.first_mention_attestation: Established as Haining County (海宁县) in 331 CE (Eastern Jin Xianhe 6; or 413 CE Yixi 9) under Yi'an Commandery, later merged into Chaoyang in early Tang.
b_haining.etymology_analysis: Auspicious coastal county name ('sea tranquility') established in Eastern Jin (331 CE) from former Jieyang territory.

historical_names.name: Jieyang
historical_names.source: Qin Shi Huang 33 (214 BCE) Jieyang Garrison
historical_names.notes: Haining was split off from ancient Jieyang County in 331 CE.

b_dongguan.first_mention_attestation: Bao'an County was renamed Dongguan County (东莞县) in 757 CE (Tang Zhide 2) under Guangzhou.
b_dongguan.etymology_analysis: Named in 757 CE for lying east of Guangzhou and producing abundant guǎn reeds (莞草), echoing the earlier Jin-dynasty Dongguan Commandery (东官郡/东莞郡).

historical_names.name: Bao'an
historical_names.source: Eastern Jin Xianhe 6 (331 CE) establishment of Bao'an County
historical_names.notes: Bao'an County was renamed Dongguan County in 757 CE.

b_baoan_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Bao'an County (宝安县) in 331 CE (Eastern Jin Xianhe 6) as seat of Dongguan Commandery.
b_baoan_1.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Eastern Jin county name ('precious peace') established in 331 CE from Panyu County, with its seat at Nantou (modern Shenzhen).

b_tunmen.first_mention_attestation: Established as Tuen Mun Military Garrison (屯门军镇) in 736 CE (Tang Kaiyuan 24) and attested in Jia Dan's Guangzhou Tonghai Yidao (New Book of Tang).
b_tunmen.etymology_analysis: Military-geographic name meaning 'garrison gate' (屯兵之门), guarding the maritime approach to Guangzhou at the mouth of the Pearl River.

b_guishan.first_mention_attestation: Xinle County was renamed Guishan County (归善县) in 589 CE (Sui Kaihuang 9) as the seat of Xunzhou.
b_guishan.etymology_analysis: Confucian-moralistic administrative name ('returning to virtue/goodness') introduced in 589 CE upon Sui unification to replace Xinle County.

historical_names.name: Xinle
historical_names.source: Eastern Jin Taihe 3 (368 CE) establishment of Xinle County from Boluo
historical_names.notes: Xinle County was renamed Guishan County in 589 CE.

b_boluo.first_mention_attestation: Earlier Fuluo County (傅罗县, 111 BCE) was renamed Boluo County (博罗县) in 280 CE (Western Jin Taikang 1).
b_boluo.etymology_analysis: Western Jin alteration (280 CE) of Han-era Fuluo (傅罗), associated with Mount Luofu (罗浮山) or a sinicized Yue substrate toponym.

historical_names.name: Fuluo
historical_names.source: Han Yuanding 6 (111 BCE) establishment under Nanhai Commandery (Hanshu Dilizhi, 2 CE)
historical_names.notes: Fuluo was renamed Boluo in 280 CE.

b_heyuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Heyuan County (河源县) in 483 CE (Southern Qi Yongming 1) under Nanhai Commandery.
b_heyuan.etymology_analysis: Geographic compound meaning 'river source', explained in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi as referring to the sources of three rivers 300 li northeast of the county seat.

b_haifeng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Haifeng County (海丰县) in 331 CE (Eastern Jin Xianhe 6) under Dongguan Commandery.
b_haifeng.etymology_analysis: Auspicious coastal county name ('abundant sea') established in 331 CE from Longchuan County.

b_luan_2.first_mention_attestation: The spelling 六安 (Lu'an) is unattested in Huizhou/Xunzhou <= 867 CE; it is a homophonous rendering of Southern Qi–early Tang Lu'an County (陆安县).
b_luan_2.etymology_analysis: 六安 (Lù'ān) is the name of an unrelated ancient state/city in Anhui; in the Huizhou/Xunzhou context it represents a homophonous graphic substitution for historical Lu'an County (陆安县, 'land peace', today in Lufeng).

historical_names.name: Lu'an
historical_names.source: Book of Southern Qi (Nan Qishu, recording counties added to Dongguan Commandery before 490 CE; abolished 627 CE)
historical_names.notes: Historical Lu'an County (陆安县) existed in Xunzhou/Dongguan from <= 490 CE until 627 CE.

b_xinle.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xinle County (欣乐县) in 368 CE (Eastern Jin Taihe 3) from Boluo County.
b_xinle.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Eastern Jin county name ('joyous and happy') established in 368 CE, later renamed Guishan County in 589 CE.

b_chengxiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Chengxiang County (程乡县) in 483 CE (Southern Qi Yongming 1) under Yi'an Commandery.
b_chengxiang.etymology_analysis: Eponymous Southern Qi county name established in 483 CE after local worthy Cheng Min (程旼), who lived in the late 5th century CE; later the seat of Meizhou.

b_likeng.first_mention_attestation: Likeng (李坑, later Likengbao in Qing-era Meixian) has no attested written record <= 867 CE.
b_likeng.etymology_analysis: Typical Hakka mountain-settlement toponym combining lǐ ('plum' or surname Li) and kēng ('gully/valley'), attested only in late imperial times (Qing-era Likengbao, modern Meixi Town).

b_songkou.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1634 CE (Ming Chongzhen 7) when Songyuan (松源) was transferred from Chengxiang County to newly created Zhenping County.
b_songkou.etymology_analysis: Named after the upper reaches of the Songyuan River (松源河) in northern Meixian; although Hakka migration there dates to the Song–Yuan period, written administrative attestation appears in Ming Chongzhen 7 (1634 CE).

b_qujiang_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Qujiang County (曲江县) in 111 BCE (Han Yuanding 6) under Guiyang Commandery, attested in Hanshu Dilizhi (2 CE).
b_qujiang_1.etymology_analysis: Hydronymic county name ('Winding River') established in 111 BCE, referring to the sharp bend of the Zhen/Wu/Beijiang river at Shaoguan.

b_lechang.first_mention_attestation: Lianghua County was renamed Lechang County (乐昌县) in 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18) under Panzhou/Shaozhou.
b_lechang.etymology_analysis: Sui-era renaming in 598 CE of Lianghua County, combining auspicious characters ('joyful and prosperous') also associated with local mountains Leishi and Changshan.

historical_names.name: Lianghua
historical_names.source: Liang dynasty (502–557 CE) establishment of Lianghua County
historical_names.notes: Lianghua County was renamed Lechang County in 598 CE.

b_wengyuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wengyuan County (翁源县) in 554 CE (Liang Chengsheng 3) under Donghengzhou Shixing Commandery.
b_wengyuan.etymology_analysis: Named in 554 CE for its location at the headwaters of the Weng River (滃江之源), a tributary of the Beijiang.

b_shixing.first_mention_attestation: Established as Shixing County (始兴县) and Shixing Commandery in 265 CE (Eastern Wu Ganlu 1).
b_shixing.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Eastern Wu administrative name ('beginning to flourish') created in 265 CE when partitioning southern Guiyang Commandery.

b_zhenchang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zhenchang County (浈昌县) in 684 CE (Tang Guangzhai 1), split from Shixing County under Shaozhou.
b_zhenchang.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county name established in 684 CE, combining the Zhen River (浈水) with auspicious chāng ('prosperous'); later renamed Baochang (保昌) in 1023 CE due to Song imperial naming taboo.

b_leixiang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Leixiang County (雷乡县) under Xunzhou in 622 CE (Tang Wude 5; also noted under Tianshou 2, 691 CE in Yuanhe Junxian Tuzhi).
b_leixiang.etymology_analysis: Tang-era county name in Longchuan/Xunzhou, combining léi ('thunder') and xiāng ('township').

b_xingning.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xingning County (兴宁县) in 331 CE (Eastern Jin Xianhe 6) under Dongguan Commandery.
b_xingning.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Eastern Jin county name ('prospering in peace') established in 331 CE from Longchuan County.

b_qichang.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Qichang County (齐昌县) added to Dongguan Commandery before 490 CE in the Book of Southern Qi (Nan Qishu), and re-established under Xunzhou in 622 CE.
b_qichang.etymology_analysis: Dynastic auspicious name ('May the Qi dynasty flourish') created under the Southern Qi (479–490 CE) in modern Wuhua/Xingning.

b_changle_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Changle County (长乐县, modern Wuhua) in 1071 CE (Northern Song Xining 4), split from Xingning County.
b_changle_1.etymology_analysis: Northern Song county name (1071 CE) derived from Changle Terrace (长乐台), a structure traditionally attributed to Nanyue King Zhao Tuo at Huacheng.

historical_names.name: Xingning
historical_names.source: Eastern Jin Xianhe 6 (331 CE) establishment of Xingning County (parent jurisdiction)
historical_names.notes: Changle County was carved out of Xingning County in 1071 CE.

b_shikeng.first_mention_attestation: Shikeng (石坑, modern Shikeng Town in Meixian/Longchuan) has no attested written record <= 867 CE.
b_shikeng.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Hakka/Cantonese topographic name meaning 'stony gully/valley', with no pre-867 CE historical attestation.

b_yangchun.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yangchun Commandery and Yangchun County (阳春县) in 523 CE (Liang Putong 4).
b_yangchun.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Southern Liang name ('sunny spring') established in 523 CE, reflecting the mild climate of the Moyang River valley.

historical_names.name: Moyang
historical_names.source: Eastern Wu Chiwu 1 (238 CE) establishment of Moyang County under Gaoxing Commandery
historical_names.notes: Moyang County (238 CE) was the earliest county established in the Yangchun area.

b_luoshui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Luoshui County (罗水县) in 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1), split from Yangchun County under Chunzhou.
b_luoshui.etymology_analysis: Hydronymic Tang county name (742 CE) named after the Luoshui River (罗水) in western Guangdong.

b_fulin.first_mention_attestation: Established as Fulin County (富林县) in 621 CE (Tang Wude 4) under Qinzhou (勤州).
b_fulin.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Tang county name ('rich forest') established in 621 CE in the Yunfu/Yangchun borderlands.

b_gaoyao.first_mention_attestation: Established as Gaoyao County (高要县) in 111 BCE (Han Yuanding 6) under Cangwu Commandery, attested in Hanshu Dilizhi (2 CE).
b_gaoyao.etymology_analysis: Han-era strategic toponym ('high strategic pass') established in 111 BCE at the Lingyang Gorge choke-point on the Xijiang River.

b_sihui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Sihui County (四会县) in 111 BCE (Han Yuanding 6) under Nanhai Commandery, attested in Hanshu Dilizhi (2 CE).
b_sihui.etymology_analysis: Hydrographic compound meaning 'confluence of four [rivers]' (Xijiang, Beijiang, Suijiang, and Longjiang), attested as a Han county since 111 BCE.

b_huameng.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Huameng County (化蒙县) under Suijian Commandery in the Book of Southern Qi (Nan Qishu, reflecting 479–490 CE administration).
b_huameng.etymology_analysis: Southern Dynasties administrative name ('civilizing the unenlightened', 启化蒙昧 — unrelated to the much later ethnonym 'Mongol'), attested in Nan Qishu (<= 490 CE) and abolished in 973 CE.

b_enping.first_mention_attestation: Qi'an County was renamed Enping County (恩平县) in 757 CE (Tang Zhide 2).
b_enping.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang renaming ('imperial grace and peace') applied in 757 CE to earlier Qi'an County (and originally Han-era Siping County, 220 CE).

historical_names.name: Siping
historical_names.source: Eastern Han Jian'an 25 (220 CE) establishment of Siping County; Southern Dynasties Qi'an County
historical_names.notes: Siping (220 CE) became Qi'an in the Southern Dynasties and was renamed Enping in 757 CE.

historical_names.name: Qi'an
historical_names.source: Eastern Han Jian'an 25 (220 CE) establishment of Siping County; Southern Dynasties Qi'an County
historical_names.notes: Siping (220 CE) became Qi'an in the Southern Dynasties and was renamed Enping in 757 CE.

b_yangjiang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yangjiang County (阳江县) in 606 CE (Sui Daye 2).
b_yangjiang.etymology_analysis: Named in 606 CE after the Moyang River (漠阳江, abbreviated Yangjiang) flowing through the county to the South China Sea.

historical_names.name: Anning
historical_names.source: Eastern Wu (220 CE) establishment of Anning County as seat of Gaoliang Commandery
historical_names.notes: Anning County (220 CE) preceded Yangjiang County at the site.

b_duling.first_mention_attestation: Established as Duling Commandery (杜陵郡) under Gaozhou in 527 CE (Liang Putong 8th year); Duyuan County was renamed Duling County in 622 CE (Tang Wude 5th year).
b_duling.etymology_analysis: Named Duling (杜陵) in 527 CE when Liang established Duling Commandery, likely echoing the prestigious Han imperial mausoleum/county name Duling near Chang'an; Duyuan County was renamed Duling County in 622 CE.

b_nanhai.first_mention_attestation: Established as Nanhai Commandery (南海郡) by the Qin dynasty in 214 BCE; Nanhai County was established in 590 CE (Sui Kaihuang 10th year).
b_nanhai.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the South China Sea (南海), first attested as a Qin commandery in 214 BCE and later as Nanhai County in 590 CE.

b_qingyuan_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Qingyuan County (清远县) in 590 CE (Sui Kaihuang 10th year), replacing the Liang-dynasty Qingyuan Commandery.
b_qingyuan_1.etymology_analysis: Named Qingyuan ('clear and distant') in the Liang/Sui period when Qingyuan Commandery and later Qingyuan County (590 CE) were established on the former Han Zhongsu County.

historical_names.name: Zhongsu
historical_names.source: Han dynasty Zhongsu County (中宿县), established in 111 BCE and recorded in Hanshu Dilizhi (2 CE).
historical_names.notes: Abolished in 590 CE when Qingyuan County was created.

b_huaiji.first_mention_attestation: Established as Huaiji County (怀集县) in 436 CE (Liu Song Yuanjia 13th year), carved from Yintun Township of Sihui.
b_huaiji.etymology_analysis: Named Huaiji ('to attract and gather [settlers/people]') upon its establishment in 436 CE during the Liu Song dynasty, also associated with the local Huai Stream (怀溪).

b_zengcheng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zengcheng County (增城县) in 201 CE (Eastern Han Jian'an 6th year), partitioned from Panyu County.
b_zengcheng.etymology_analysis: Named Zengcheng ('added walled city') in 201 CE because Nanhai Commandery previously had six counties and adding a new county increased the number of walled seats by one.

b_xiangshan_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xiangshan County (香山县) in 1152 CE (Southern Song Shaoxing 22nd year) from the earlier Xiangshan Garrison (香山寨).
b_xiangshan_1.etymology_analysis: Named after Xiangshan (Fragrant Mountain, modern Wugui Mountain area); elevated to Xiangshan County in 1152 CE and renamed Zhongshan in 1925 CE.

b_duanxi.first_mention_attestation: Established as Duanxi County (端溪县) in 111 BCE (Western Han Yuanding 6th year) under Cangwu Commandery, recorded in Hanshu Dilizhi (2 CE).
b_duanxi.etymology_analysis: Named after the Duan Stream (端溪) within its territory, established as a county in 111 BCE and later serving as the seat of Kangzhou (modern Deqing).

b_yuecheng_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yuecheng County (悦城县) during the Liu Song dynasty (420–479 CE), abolished in 592 CE, and restored in 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1st year).
b_yuecheng_1.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name ('pleasing walled town') first established under Jinkang Commandery in the Liu Song dynasty (420–479 CE) and restored in 742 CE from Lecheng County.

b_fengchuan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Fengchuan County (封川县) from Liangxin County in 598 CE (Sui Kaihuang 18th year).
b_fengchuan.etymology_analysis: Named Fengchuan ('river of Feng[zhou]') in 598 CE when Sui renamed Liangxin County as the seat of Fengzhou.

historical_names.name: Guangxin
historical_names.source: Western Han Guangxin County (广信县), established 111 BCE, later Liangxin County (梁信县).
historical_names.notes: Renamed Fengchuan County in 598 CE.

historical_names.name: Liangxin
historical_names.source: Western Han Guangxin County (广信县), established 111 BCE, later Liangxin County (梁信县).
historical_names.notes: Renamed Fengchuan County in 598 CE.

b_kaijian.first_mention_attestation: Established as Kaijian County (开建县) in 426 CE (Liu Song Yuanjia 3rd year), partitioned from Fengyang County.
b_kaijian.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name ('open and establish') given when the county was newly partitioned from Fengyang in 426 CE.

b_shuangshui.first_mention_attestation: Longzhou (泷州) was established in 508 CE (Liang Tianjian 7th year) and Longxiang County was renamed Longshui County (泷水县) in the Sui/Liang period.
b_shuangshui.etymology_analysis: Named after the Longshui (modern Luoding River), whose rocky rapids ('longhou') gave the river and county their name.

historical_names.name: Longxiang
historical_names.source: Eastern Jin Yuanxi 1st year (419 CE) establishment of Longxiang County (龙乡县).
historical_names.notes: Longxiang was the predecessor county renamed Longshui.

b_jinshui_1.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Jianshui County (建水县) from Yongning County in 742 CE (Tang Tianbao 1st year) under Kaiyang Commandery (Longzhou).
b_jinshui_1.etymology_analysis: Named Jianshui in 742 CE after the local Jian River (from earlier Jianzhou / Yongning County), merged into Longshui County in 973 CE.

historical_names.name: Yongning
historical_names.source: Yongning County (永宁县), transferred to Longzhou in 644 CE.
historical_names.notes: Renamed Jianshui in 742 CE.

b_jinkang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jinkang Commandery (晋康郡) in 351 CE (Eastern Jin Yonghe 7th year); Ansui County was renamed Jinkang County in 756 CE (Tang Zhide 1st year).
b_jinkang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious dynastic name ('Jin dynasty peace/prosperity') created when Eastern Jin established Jinkang Commandery in 351 CE, later applied to Jinkang County in 756 CE.

b_zhennan.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Zhennan County (镇南县) from Annan County in 757 CE (Tang Zhide 2nd year) under Longzhou.
b_zhennan.etymology_analysis: Imperial garrison name ('Pacifying the South') given in 757 CE when Tang renamed Annan County under Longzhou.

historical_names.name: Annan
historical_names.source: Annan County (安南县), placed under Longzhou in 644 CE.
historical_names.notes: Renamed Zhennan County in 757 CE.

b_xinxing.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xinxing County (新兴县) in 351 CE (Eastern Jin Yonghe 7th year) under Xinning Commandery.
b_xinxing.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name ('newly flourishing') given upon the county's creation in 351 CE.

historical_names.name: Linyun
historical_names.source: Han Linyun County (临允县, 111 BCE) and Western Jin Xinning County (新宁县).
historical_names.notes: Xinxing County was carved out under Xinning Commandery in 351 CE.

historical_names.name: Xinning
historical_names.source: Han Linyun County (临允县, 111 BCE) and Western Jin Xinning County (新宁县).
historical_names.notes: Xinxing County was carved out under Xinning Commandery in 351 CE.

b_pingxing.first_mention_attestation: Established as Pingxing County (平兴县) in 351 CE (Eastern Jin Yonghe 7th year) under Jinkang/Xinning Commandery, later under Duanzhou.
b_pingxing.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name ('peaceful and flourishing') established in 351 CE during the Eastern Jin dynasty.

b_yongshun.first_mention_attestation: Yongshun County (永顺县) is attested under Xinzhou in Tang administrative geography (Old Book of Tang / New Book of Tang, Xinzhou established 621 CE).
b_yongshun.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name ('perpetually compliant/harmonious') used for a Tang county under Xinzhou in Lingnan Circuit.

b_xinhui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Xinhui Commandery (新会郡) in 420 CE (Eastern Jin Yuanxi 2nd year).
b_xinhui.etymology_analysis: Named Xinhui ('new convergence') in 420 CE when Eastern Jin created Xinhui Commandery from Pingyi and surrounding lands.

historical_names.name: Pingyi
historical_names.source: Eastern Wu Pingyi County (平夷县), established in 222 CE.
historical_names.notes: Predecessor county in the Xinhui area prior to 420 CE.

b_zhenyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Zhenyang County (浈阳县) in 111 BCE (Western Han Yuanding 6th year), recorded in Hanshu Dilizhi (2 CE).

morphemes.translation: north bank of a river, sunny side

b_zhenyang.etymology_analysis: Directional/locator compound meaning 'north (yang) bank of the Zhen River', established as a Western Han county in 111 BCE.

b_hankuang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Hankuang County (含洭县, later written 浛洭县) in 111 BCE (Western Han Yuanding 6th year), recorded in Hanshu Dilizhi (2 CE).
b_hankuang.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kuang River (洭水) where it joins the Beijiang, established in 111 BCE as Han's Hankuang County.

b_yilun.first_mention_attestation: Established as Yilun County (义伦县) in 610 CE (Sui Daye 6th year) as the seat of Dan'er Commandery.
b_yilun.etymology_analysis: Confucian moralizing name ('righteousness and social order') given by the Sui dynasty in 610 CE on the site of ancient Dan'er County.

historical_names.name: Dan'er
historical_names.source: Western Han Dan'er Commandery/County (儋耳), established in 110 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Yilun County was built on the old Han Dan'er County seat.

b_changhua_1.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Changhua County (昌化县) in 610 CE (Sui Daye 6th year) under Dan'er Commandery.
b_changhua_1.etymology_analysis: Imperial civilizing name ('prosperous transformation') established by the Sui dynasty in 610 CE on western Hainan.

historical_names.name: Zhilai
historical_names.source: Western Han Zhilai County (至来县, 110 BCE) under Dan'er Commandery.
historical_names.notes: Zhilai County was located at modern Changhua's Jiuxian village.

b_ganen.first_mention_attestation: Established as Gan'en County (感恩县) in 607 CE (Sui Daye 3rd year) under Zhuya Commandery.
b_ganen.etymology_analysis: Imperial pacification name ('grateful for imperial grace') established by the Sui dynasty in 607 CE on southwestern Hainan.

b_liodong.first_mention_attestation: The term Lidong (黎峒, Li mountain settlements/gorges) is attested in Song dynasty writings from the late 11th century (Su Shi's Hainan exile, 1097–1100 CE) and 12th-century gazetteers.
b_liodong.etymology_analysis: Ethno-topographic term denoting the autonomous mountain valley settlements (dong) of the indigenous Li (Hlai) people in interior Hainan, documented from the Song dynasty onward.

b_limu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Limu Mountain (黎母山) in Zhou Qufei's Lingwai Daida (1178 CE, Song dynasty).
b_limu.etymology_analysis: Named after Limu Mountain (黎母山, 'Ancestral Mother of the Li') in central Hainan, first documented in Song-era geographical works such as Lingwai Daida (1178 CE).

b_chengmai.first_mention_attestation: Established as Chengmai County (澄迈县) in 607 CE (Sui Daye 3rd year) on the site of former Gouzhong County.
b_chengmai.etymology_analysis: Named Chengmai (澄迈) in 607 CE during the Sui dynasty, replacing the Western Han Gouzhong County on northern Hainan (adapted in the repository as the semantic calque 'Luterweit').

historical_names.name: Gouzhong
historical_names.source: Western Han Gouzhong County (苟中县), established in 110 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Chengmai County was established in 607 CE on the old Gouzhong County site.

b_wanan_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Wan'an County (万安县) in 631 CE (Tang Zhenguan 5th year), partitioned from Pingchang County under Qiongzhou.
b_wanan_1.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name ('myriad peace') established in 631 CE and elevated to Wan'an Prefecture in 662 CE (modern Wanning).

b_lehui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lehui County (乐会县) in 660 CE (Tang Xianqing 5th year) under Qiongzhou.
b_lehui.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name ('joyful gathering') established in 660 CE on eastern Hainan (modern Qionghai).

b_lingshui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lingshui County (陵水县) in 610 CE (Sui Daye 6th year) under Linzhen Commandery.
b_lingshui.etymology_analysis: Named after the Lingshui River (陵水河) flowing through the county to the sea, established in 610 CE.

b_shecheng.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Shecheng County (舍城县) from Wude County in 610 CE (Sui Daye 6th year) under Zhuya Commandery.
b_shecheng.etymology_analysis: Administrative name ('lodging walled town') given in 610 CE when Sui renamed Wude County in northern Hainan.

historical_names.name: Wude
historical_names.source: Sui Daye 3rd year (607 CE) Wude County (武德县).
historical_names.notes: Renamed Shecheng County in 610 CE.

b_siqiongshan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Qiongshan County (琼山县) in 627 CE (Tang Zhenguan 1st year), partitioned from Shecheng County.
b_siqiongshan.etymology_analysis: Named after Qiongshan ('Jade Mountain') in Baishidu, where the soil and stones were described as white and lustrous like jade.

b_wenchang.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Wenchang County (文昌县) from Pingchang County in 627 CE (Tang Zhenguan 1st year).
b_wenchang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious administrative name ('flourishing culture/letters') given in 627 CE when Pingchang County was renamed.

historical_names.name: Pingchang
historical_names.source: Tang Wude 5th year (622 CE) Pingchang County (平昌县).
historical_names.notes: Renamed Wenchang County in 627 CE.

b_ningyuan.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ningyuan County (宁远县) under Zhuya Commandery in the Book of Sui (610 CE, Sui Daye 6th year).
b_ningyuan.etymology_analysis: Frontier pacification name ('pacifying the distant [regions]'), also associated with the Ningyuan River in southern Hainan (modern Yazhou, Sanya).

b_yande.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Yande County (延德县) under Zhuya Commandery in the Book of Sui (610 CE, Sui Daye 6th year).
b_yande.etymology_analysis: Confucian imperial name ('extending imperial virtue') established by the Sui dynasty on southern Hainan under Zhuya/Zhenzhou.

b_jiyang.first_mention_attestation: Established as Jiyang County (吉阳县) in 628 CE (Tang Zhenguan 2nd year), partitioned from Yande County under Zhenzhou (Old Book of Tang).
b_jiyang.etymology_analysis: Auspicious name ('auspicious sunlight') given when the county was created on southern Hainan in 628 CE (modern Jiyang District, Sanya).

b_lingui.first_mention_attestation: Shi'an County was renamed Lingui County (临桂县) in 634 CE (Tang Zhenguan 8th year; also recorded in 757 CE under Guizhou).
b_lingui.etymology_analysis: Directional/locator compound meaning 'bordering the Gui River' (or Guizhou), renamed from Shi'an County in the Tang dynasty.

historical_names.name: Shi'an
historical_names.source: Western Han Shi'an County (始安县), established in 111 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Renamed Lingui County in the Tang dynasty.

b_lingchuan.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lingchuan County (灵川县) in 621 CE (Tang Wude 4th year), partitioned from Shi'an County (Old Book of Tang).
b_lingchuan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Lingqu Canal / Ling River system ('numinous stream') in northeastern Guangxi when established in 621 CE.

b_lipu.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lipu County (荔浦县) in 111 BCE (Western Han Yuanding 6th year) under Cangwu Commandery, recorded in Hanshu Dilizhi (2 CE).
b_lipu.etymology_analysis: Named after the Lipu River (荔浦水), a tributary bank where wild lychee grew, attested since 111 BCE.

b_liding.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Liding County (理定县) from Xing'an County in 757 CE (Tang Zhide 2nd year) under Guizhou.
b_liding.etymology_analysis: Administrative pacification name ('govern and stabilize') given in 757 CE when Tang renamed Xing'an County (later merged into Yongfu County in 1440 CE).

historical_names.name: Xing'an
historical_names.source: Sui Kaihuang-era Xing'an County (兴安县).
historical_names.notes: Renamed Liding County in 757 CE.

b_maping.first_mention_attestation: Established as Maping Commandery (马平郡) in 540 CE (Liang Datong 6th year); Tanzhong County was renamed Maping County in 591 CE (Sui Kaihuang 11th year).
b_maping.etymology_analysis: Named Maping ('horse plain') in 540 CE as a Liang commandery and in 591 CE as the seat county of Liuzhou.

historical_names.name: Tanzhong
historical_names.source: Western Han Tanzhong County (潭中县), established in 111 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Tanzhong was renamed Guilin and then Maping in 591 CE.

b_luorong.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Luorong County (洛容县) in Tang administrative records of Guizhou (668 CE) and later transferred to Liuzhou in 691 CE.
b_luorong.etymology_analysis: Named after the Luo River (洛水 / Luoqing River) in northern Guangxi, attested as a Tang county in Guizhou and Liuzhou by the late 7th century.

b_luocao.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Luocao County (洛曹县) from Luofeng County in 818 CE (Tang Yuanhe 13th year) under Liuzhou.
b_luocao.etymology_analysis: Renamed from Luofeng County in 818 CE, combining the Luo River hydronym with the local Cao settlement name (modern Dacao Village, Yizhou).

historical_names.name: Luofeng
historical_names.source: Tang Qianfeng 3rd year (668 CE) Luofeng County (洛封县).
historical_names.notes: Renamed Luocao County in 818 CE.

b_longcheng_1.first_mention_attestation: Established as Longcheng County (龙城县) in 537 CE (Liang Datong 3rd year), renamed Liucheng County in 1006 CE.
b_longcheng_1.etymology_analysis: Named Longcheng ('Dragon City', referencing the Longjiang River and local dragon lore) when established in 537 CE.

b_longshui.first_mention_attestation: Established as Longshui County (龙水县) in 630 CE (Tang Zhenguan 4th year) as the seat of Yuezhou (later Yizhou).
b_longshui.etymology_analysis: Named after the Longjiang River (龙水) flowing past the county seat in modern Yizhou, Hechi, established in 630 CE.

b_dumeng.first_mention_attestation: Established as Dumeng County (都蒙县, also written Mengdu 蒙都县) in 638 CE (Tang Zhenguan 12th year) under Huanzhou in modern Huanjiang/Yizhou.
b_dumeng.etymology_analysis: Chinese phonetic transcription of a native Kra-Dai (Zhuang/Maonan) place name in northern Guangxi, attested as a county of Huanzhou from 638 CE.

b_yimeng.first_mention_attestation: Established in 638 CE (12th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Si'en County under Huanzhou (Huanzhou Zhengping Commandery), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_yimeng.etymology_analysis: Si'en (思恩) is a Tang-era auspicious administrative name meaning 'remembering imperial grace,' given when Li Hongjie pacified the local Man/Liao communities and established Huanzhou in 638 CE.

b_rongshui.first_mention_attestation: Named Rongshui County in 623 CE (6th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) when Yixi County was renamed Rongshui, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a) and Liuzhou municipal records.
b_rongshui.etymology_analysis: Rongshui (融水) is named after the Rong River (融水 / 融江), which flows through the county; in 623 CE, Tang authorities renamed the earlier Yixi County to Rongshui County.

historical_names.name: Yixi
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a) and Suishu, recording Yixi County as seat of Rongzhou in 598 CE
historical_names.notes: Yixi County served as the seat of Rongzhou from 598 CE until it was renamed Rongshui County in 623 CE.

b_wuyang_1.first_mention_attestation: Established in 742 CE (early Tianbao era, Tang dynasty) by merging Huangshui and Linzang counties into Wuyang County under Rongzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_wuyang_1.etymology_analysis: Wuyang (武阳) is a Tang-era auspicious/topographic compound combining 'martial' (武) and 'sunny side' (阳), created in 742 CE when Huangshui and Linzang counties were consolidated.

historical_names.name: Linzang
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a), recording Linzang and Huangshui counties established in 621 CE
historical_names.notes: Linzang and Huangshui counties were established in 621 CE under Rongzhou and merged to form Wuyang County in 742 CE.

historical_names.name: Huangshui
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a), recording Linzang and Huangshui counties established in 621 CE
historical_names.notes: Linzang and Huangshui counties were established in 621 CE under Rongzhou and merged to form Wuyang County in 742 CE.

b_leshan_2.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in the Songshi Geography Treatise (地理志) as Leshanzhou (乐善州), a jimi prefecture that submitted under Northern Song in Yongxi 3 (986 CE) and is described in Songshi as a former Tang prefecture (no dated pre-867 CE attestation survives).
b_leshan_2.etymology_analysis: Leshan (乐善) is an auspicious Chinese administrative name meaning 'delighting in goodness,' attested for a Song-era jimi prefecture subordinate to Rongzhou and Shaoqingfu.

b_yangshou.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 592 CE (12th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) when Xiangzhou was established over Guilin and Yangshou counties, recorded in Suishu and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_yangshou.etymology_analysis: Yangshou (阳寿) is an auspicious Sui-era county name combining 'sunny/yang' (阳) and 'longevity' (寿), serving as the seat of Xiangzhou from 776 CE.

b_wuxian.first_mention_attestation: Established in 621 CE (4th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) by splitting Guilin County under Xiangzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_wuxian.etymology_analysis: Wuxian (武仙) was created in 621 CE alongside Wude and Wuhua as one of three 'Wu-' counties in Xiangzhou, combining 'martial' (武) and 'immortal' (仙); it was later renamed Wuxuan in 1431 CE.

historical_names.name: Guilin
historical_names.source: Xiangzhou (ancient) records (Guilin County served as Sui Xiangzhou seat in 591 CE)
historical_names.notes: Wuxian County was carved out of Guilin County in 621 CE.

b_laibin.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Laibin County in 743 CE (2nd year of Tianbao, Tang dynasty) from Huaiyi County, recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Zhi.
b_laibin.etymology_analysis: Laibin (来宾) derives from the classical phrase 'coming as honored guests' (来宾), reflecting Tang pacification and incorporation of local populations along the Hongshui/Qianjiang basin.

historical_names.name: Huaiyi
historical_names.source: Laibin City historical records / Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a), noting Yanzhou and Huaiyi County established in 667 CE
historical_names.notes: Huaiyi County was established in 667 CE and renamed Laibin County in 743 CE.

b_pingnan.first_mention_attestation: Established in 633 CE (7th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Pingnan County under Gongzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_pingnan.etymology_analysis: Pingnan (平南) means 'pacifying the south,' an imperial Tang administrative name coined when Gongzhou was established in 633 CE.

historical_names.name: Wucheng
historical_names.source: Pingnan County historical records (Western Jin split Mengling to form Wucheng County c. 280 CE)
historical_names.notes: The area was part of Mengling in Han and Wucheng from early Western Jin prior to Tang Pingnan.

b_wulang.first_mention_attestation: Named Lishan County in 622 CE (5th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) from Suihua County under Nan'gongzhou (later Mengzhou), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_wulang.etymology_analysis: Lishan (立山, 'Standing Mountain') was named in 622 CE after Mount Li in modern Mengshan County, replacing the Sui-era name Suihua.

historical_names.name: Suihua
historical_names.source: Mengshan County historical records / Xin Tangshu (Suihua County established 590 CE)
historical_names.notes: Suihua County was established in 590 CE and renamed Lishan County in 622 CE.

b_wulin.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Wulin County in 425 CE (2nd year of Yuanjia, Liu Song dynasty) from Wucheng County under Yongping Commandery, recorded in Songshu and Taiping Huanyu Ji (Vol. 158).
b_wulin.etymology_analysis: Wulin (武林, 'Martial Woods') arose in 425 CE as a Liu Song renaming of Wucheng County under Yongping Commandery, later transferred from Tengzhou to Gongzhou in the early Tang.

historical_names.name: Wucheng
historical_names.source: Jinshu / Pingnan historical records (Wucheng County established c. 280 CE)
historical_names.notes: Wucheng County was renamed Wulin County in 425 CE.

b_cangwu.first_mention_attestation: Cangwu Commandery (苍梧郡) was established in 111 BCE (6th year of Yuanding, Western Han) following the conquest of Nanyue, recorded in Hanshu (Dilizhi); the county itself took the name Cangwu in 583 CE.
b_cangwu.etymology_analysis: Cangwu (苍梧) is a classical regional choronym (originally associated with the southern wilds of Shun in Warring States texts) applied by Zhao Tuo and Western Han to Cangwu Commandery in 111 BCE, and to Cangwu County (formerly Guangxin) in 583 CE.

b_linhe_1.first_mention_attestation: Established in 111 BCE (6th year of Yuanding, Western Han) as Linhe County under Cangwu Commandery, recorded in Hanshu (Dilizhi).
b_linhe_1.etymology_analysis: Linhe (临贺) is a locator compound meaning 'overlooking the He River' (referring to the confluence of the Lin and He rivers), as noted in Shuijingzhu.

b_fuchuan_1.first_mention_attestation: Established in 111 BCE (6th year of Yuanding, Western Han) as Fuchuan County under Cangwu Commandery, recorded in Hanshu (Dilizhi).
b_fuchuan_1.etymology_analysis: Fuchuan (富川) is named after the Fuchuan River (富川江) flowing through the valley between the Dupang and Mengzhu ranges.

b_pingle.first_mention_attestation: Named Yongping County in 591 CE (11th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) when Funing County was renamed Yongping under Tengzhou, later transferred to Zhaozhou in the Tang dynasty, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_pingle.etymology_analysis: Yongping (永平, 'Eternal Peace') is an auspicious Sui-era administrative name given in 591 CE to replace Funing County, later serving as a county of Zhaozhou.

historical_names.name: Funing
historical_names.source: Tengzhou / Suishu administrative records (Funing County renamed Yongping in 591 CE)
historical_names.notes: Funing County was renamed Yongping County in 591 CE.

b_yangshuo.first_mention_attestation: Named Gongcheng County in 621 CE (4th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) from Chacheng County under Lezhou (later Zhaozhou), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_yangshuo.etymology_analysis: Gongcheng (恭城, 'Reverent City') was renamed by Tang authorities in 621 CE from Chacheng County, which Xiao Xian had split from Pingle in 618 CE.

historical_names.name: Chacheng
historical_names.source: Gongcheng County gazetteer (Xiao Xian established Chacheng County in 618 CE)
historical_names.notes: Chacheng County was established in 618 CE and renamed Gongcheng County in 621 CE.

b_longpimg.first_mention_attestation: Attested by 607 CE (Daye 3, Sui dynasty) as Longping County under Shi'an Commandery, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 31) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_longpimg.etymology_analysis: Longping (龙平) is an auspicious Chinese toponym combining 'dragon' (龙) and 'peace/plain' (平), serving as the seat of Jingzhou/Fuzhou in Tang before being renamed Zhaoping in 1124 CE.

b_bobai.first_mention_attestation: Established in 621 CE (4th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) as Bobai County under Nanzhou (renamed Baizhou in 623 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_bobai.etymology_analysis: Bobai (博白) is named after the Bobai River (博白江, modern Xiaobai River), established in 621 CE by splitting Nanchang County.

historical_names.name: Nanchang
historical_names.source: Southern Chen / Bobai County historical records (split from Nanchang County in 621 CE)
historical_names.notes: Bobai County was carved out of Nanchang County in 621 CE.

b_zhouluo.first_mention_attestation: Established in 621 CE (4th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) as Zhouluo County under Nanzhou (later Baizhou), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_zhouluo.etymology_analysis: Zhouluo (周罗) is a Tang-era county name established in 621 CE under Nanzhou/Baizhou, likely reflecting a sinicized local toponym or administrative designation.

b_longchi.first_mention_attestation: Established in 686 CE (2nd year of Chuigong, Tang dynasty) as Longchi County, seat of Shanzhou (renamed Longchi Commandery in 742 CE), recorded in Shanzhou / Jiu Tangshu.
b_longchi.etymology_analysis: Longchi (龙池, 'Dragon Pool') was established in 686 CE as the seat of Shanzhou in southwestern Bobai, named after a local pool feature.

b_hepu_1.first_mention_attestation: Established in 111 BCE (6th year of Yuanding, Western Han) as Hepu Commandery and Hepu County, recorded in Hanshu (Dilizhi).
b_hepu_1.etymology_analysis: Hepu (合浦) is a descriptive Chinese compound meaning 'converging estuaries/waters,' referring to the coastal river mouths along the Beibu Gulf where the Nanliu River meets the sea.

b_dalian.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Southern Chen dynasty (557–589 CE) as Dalian County under Longsu Commandery of Yuezhou, and re-established in 622 CE under Lianzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_dalian.etymology_analysis: Dalian (大廉) derives from the Dalian Cave/Mountain region (大廉洞), which also gave its name to Lianzhou when Yuezhou was renamed Lianzhou in 634 CE.

b_fengshan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Southern Chen dynasty (557–589 CE) as Fengshan County, seat of Fengshan Commandery under Yuezhou, and in Suishu (Vol. 31) under Hepu Commandery.
b_fengshan.etymology_analysis: Fengshan (封山) is named after Mount Feng (封山) on the borderlands of ancient Lingshan and Pubei.

b_puning_1.first_mention_attestation: Named Puning County in 599 CE (19th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) when Fenghua County was renamed Puning under Yongping Commandery, recorded in Rong County records and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_puning_1.etymology_analysis: Puning (普宁, 'Universal Tranquility') is an auspicious Sui-era county name given in 599 CE, which later served as the Tang commandery name (Puning Commandery) for Rongzhou.

historical_names.name: Fenghua
historical_names.source: Rong County historical records (Western Jin Dangchang County; Southern Liang Yinshi County 523 CE; Sui Fenghua renamed Puning 599 CE)
historical_names.notes: Western Jin Dangchang County was renamed Yinshi in 523 CE, later Fenghua, and Puning in 599 CE.

historical_names.name: Dangchang
historical_names.source: Rong County historical records (Western Jin Dangchang County; Southern Liang Yinshi County 523 CE; Sui Fenghua renamed Puning 599 CE)
historical_names.notes: Western Jin Dangchang County was renamed Yinshi in 523 CE, later Fenghua, and Puning in 599 CE.

historical_names.name: Yinshi
historical_names.source: Rong County historical records (Western Jin Dangchang County; Southern Liang Yinshi County 523 CE; Sui Fenghua renamed Puning 599 CE)
historical_names.notes: Western Jin Dangchang County was renamed Yinshi in 523 CE, later Fenghua, and Puning in 599 CE.

b_beiliu.first_mention_attestation: Established in 488 CE (6th year of Yongming, Southern Qi dynasty) as Beiliu Commandery, and attested as Beiliu County in Suishu (Vol. 31) and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_beiliu.etymology_analysis: Beiliu (北流, 'North-Flowing') is named after the Beiliu River (北流江), which flows northward into the Xunjiang/Xijiang system.

b_longhua.first_mention_attestation: Established in 621 CE (4th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) as Longhua County (later seat of Shunzhou in 773 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_longhua.etymology_analysis: Longhua (龙化) is explicitly noted in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a) as taking its name from the Longhua River (龙化水) to its west.

b_luchuan_1.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Southern Qi dynasty (479–502 CE, c. 488 CE) as Luchuan Commandery (陆川郡) under Yuezhou, and as Luchuan County under Southern Chen and Tang, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_luchuan_1.etymology_analysis: Luchuan (陆川, 'Land and Stream') is a Southern Dynasties administrative name for the upper Jiuzhou River basin in southeastern Guangxi.

b_tanjin.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Tang dynasty (replacing Yongping as the seat of Tengzhou by the Tianbao era, 742 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_tanjin.etymology_analysis: Tanjin (镡津, 'Sword-Guard Ford') is named after the historic river crossing and rapids at the confluence near Tengzhou.

historical_names.name: Yongping
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a), noting Tengzhou originally governed Yongping before Tanjin was established
historical_names.notes: Yongping County was the earlier seat of Tengzhou before being transferred to Zhaozhou and succeeded by Tanjin.

b_rongcheng_1.first_mention_attestation: Named Rongcheng County in 599 CE (19th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) when Suicheng County was renamed Rongcheng, recorded in Cangwu County records and Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_rongcheng_1.etymology_analysis: Rongcheng (戎城, 'Military Citadel') was coined in 599 CE as a Sui renaming of Suicheng County, originally founded as Nongcheng in 280 CE.

historical_names.name: Nongcheng
historical_names.source: Cangwu County historical records (Nongcheng established 280 CE, renamed Suicheng in Eastern Jin)
historical_names.notes: Established as Nongcheng in 280 CE, renamed Suicheng in Eastern Jin, and renamed Rongcheng in 599 CE.

historical_names.name: Suicheng
historical_names.source: Cangwu County historical records (Nongcheng established 280 CE, renamed Suicheng in Eastern Jin)
historical_names.notes: Established as Nongcheng in 280 CE, renamed Suicheng in Eastern Jin, and renamed Rongcheng in 599 CE.

b_cenxi.first_mention_attestation: Named Cenxi County in 757 CE (2nd year of Zhide, Tang dynasty) when Longcheng County was renamed Cenxi, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_cenxi.etymology_analysis: Cenxi (岑溪) was named in 757 CE after the Cen Stream (岑水 / 岑溪) flowing through the county.

historical_names.name: Longcheng
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a), noting Longcheng County was established in 622 CE and renamed Cenxi in 757 CE
historical_names.notes: Longcheng County was established in 622 CE under Nanyizhou and renamed Cenxi in 757 CE.

b_yuping.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Western Jin dynasty (280 CE) as Yuping County under Yulin Commandery, recorded in Jinshu (Vol. 15).
b_yuping.etymology_analysis: Yuping (郁平) combines 'Yu' (from Yulin Commandery) and 'ping' (plain/peaceful), serving as a major county of Yulin Commandery and later Yulin Prefecture.

historical_names.name: Guangdu
historical_names.source: Yulin historical records (Han Guangdu County preceded Yuping)
historical_names.notes: Earlier Han-era Guangdu County was renamed Yuping by the Western Jin.

b_xingye.first_mention_attestation: Established in 665 CE (2nd year of Linde, Tang dynasty) by splitting Shinan County under Yulin Prefecture, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_xingye.etymology_analysis: Xingye (兴业, 'Prospering Enterprise') is an auspicious Tang-era administrative name coined when the county was created in 665 CE.

historical_names.name: Shinan
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a) and Suishu (Shinan County existed prior to 665 CE)
historical_names.notes: Xingye County was split from Shinan County in 665 CE, and Shinan was later merged into Xingye in 781 CE.

b_nanliu.first_mention_attestation: Established in 621 CE (4th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) by splitting Beiliu County under Rongzhou (later seat of Laozhou), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_nanliu.etymology_analysis: Nanliu (南流, 'South-Flowing') is explicitly noted in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a) as named after the Nanliu River (南流江) a hundred paces to its south.

historical_names.name: Beiliu
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a), noting Nanliu was split from Beiliu in 621 CE
historical_names.notes: Nanliu County was carved out of Beiliu County in 621 CE.

b_lingfang.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Hanshu (Dilizhi, 2 CE census) as Lingfang County (领方县) under Yulin Commandery, later written 岭方.
b_lingfang.etymology_analysis: Lingfang (领方 / 岭方) is a Han-era county name in Yulin Commandery, likely a sinicized transcription of a local Yue/Tai-Kadai toponym or referring to the mountain-pass region.

b_shanglin.first_mention_attestation: Established in 621 CE (4th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) from Shanglin Dong of Lingfang County under Nanfangzhou (later Chengzhou), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_shanglin.etymology_analysis: Shanglin (上林, 'Upper Forest') derives from the local Shanglin Dong (上林峒) valley settlement in Lingfang County, elevated to a county in 621 CE.

historical_names.name: Lingfang
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a), noting Shanglin was split from Lingfang County in 621 CE
historical_names.notes: Shanglin County was split from Lingfang County in 621 CE.

b_heshui.first_mention_attestation: Established in 621 CE (4th year of Wude, Tang dynasty) by splitting Maping County under Liuzhou, later transferred to Chengzhou in 624 CE, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_heshui.etymology_analysis: Heshui (贺水) is named after the He River (贺水) in the Shanglin–Liujiang borderlands, and also gave its name to Heshui Commandery (Chengzhou) in 742 CE.

historical_names.name: Maping
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a), noting Heshui was split from Maping County in 621 CE
historical_names.notes: Heshui County was carved out of Maping County in 621 CE.

b_ningpu.first_mention_attestation: Established by 286 CE (7th year of Taikang, Western Jin) as Ningpu County and seat of Ningpu Commandery, recorded in Jinshu (Vol. 15) and Songshu.
b_ningpu.etymology_analysis: Ningpu (宁浦, 'Tranquil Riverbank') is a Wu/Western Jin-era administrative name along the Yu River (郁江) in modern Hengzhou.

historical_names.name: An'guang
historical_names.source: Hengzhou City historical records (Han An'guang and Pingshan counties preceded Ningpu)
historical_names.notes: Han-era An'guang and Pingshan counties occupied the Hengzhou area before Ningpu was established.

historical_names.name: Pingshan
historical_names.source: Hengzhou City historical records (Han An'guang and Pingshan counties preceded Ningpu)
historical_names.notes: Han-era An'guang and Pingshan counties occupied the Hengzhou area before Ningpu was established.

b_yongding.first_mention_attestation: Established in 621 CE (early Wude era, Tang dynasty) as Yongding County, seat of Chunzhou (renamed Luanzhou in 805 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_yongding.etymology_analysis: Yongding (永定, 'Eternal Stability') is an auspicious Tang-era administrative name coined when Chunzhou was established in 621 CE.

b_qinjiang.first_mention_attestation: Named Qinjiang County in 598 CE (18th year of Kaihuang, Sui dynasty) when Songshou County was renamed Qinjiang alongside Qinzhou, recorded in Suishu (Vol. 31) and Yuanhe Junxian Zhi.
b_qinjiang.etymology_analysis: Qinjiang (钦江) is named after the Qin River (钦江), as recorded in Yuanhe Junxian Zhi.

historical_names.name: Songshou
historical_names.source: Suishu (Vol. 31) / Qinzhou historical records (Liu Song Songshou Commandery/County renamed Qinjiang in 598 CE)
historical_names.notes: Songshou County was renamed Qinjiang County in 598 CE.

b_lingshan.first_mention_attestation: Named Lingshan County in 636 CE (10th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) when Nanbin County was renamed Lingshan, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_lingshan.etymology_analysis: Lingshan (灵山, 'Numinous Mountain') was named in 636 CE after Xilingshan (modern Liufeng Mountain) at the county seat.

historical_names.name: Nanbin
historical_names.source: Lingshan County historical records / Xin Tangshu (Nanbin County established 598 CE)
historical_names.notes: Nanbin County was established in 598 CE and renamed Lingshan County in 636 CE.

b_anjing.first_mention_attestation: Named Baojing County in 757 CE (2nd year of Zhide, Tang dynasty) when Anjing County was renamed Baojing under Qinzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_anjing.etymology_analysis: Baojing (保京, 'Protecting the Capital') was coined in 757 CE during the An Lushan Rebellion as an auspicious renaming of Anjing County (established 589 CE).

historical_names.name: Anjing
historical_names.source: Qinzhou historical records / Xin Tangshu (Anjing County established 589 CE)
historical_names.notes: Anjing County was established in 589 CE and renamed Baojing in 757 CE (later reverted to Anjing in early Song).

b_rangjiang.first_mention_attestation: Established in 638 CE (12th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Rangjiang County (written Linjiang in Jiu Tangshu) under Rangzhou, recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_rangjiang.etymology_analysis: Rangjiang (瀼江) is named after the Rang River in southern Guangxi (modern Shangsi/Chongzuo area), serving as the seat of Tang Rangzhou.

b_wule.first_mention_attestation: Established in 638 CE (12th year of Zhenguan, Tang dynasty) as Wuqin County (written Wule 武勒 in Jiu Tangshu, Tongdian, and Taiping Huanyu Ji), seat of Longzhou (笼州), recorded in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43a).
b_wule.etymology_analysis: Wuqin (武勤) is the Xin Tangshu textual variant of Wule (武勒), the Tang-era seat of Longzhou established in 638 CE by Li Hongjie.

b_xianchuan.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b, compiled 1060 CE) as the sole county of Simingzhou (思明州), a jimi prefecture under Yongzhou Dudufu, with no specific establishment year recorded.
b_xianchuan.etymology_analysis: Xianchuan (显川, 'Illustrious Stream') is an auspicious administrative name for the county under Simingzhou on the Guangxi–Vietnam borderlands, attested only in the Song-compiled Xin Tangshu.

b_shukun.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1371 CE (4th year of Hongwu, Ming dynasty) as Shukun Township (述昆乡), transferred from Shanglin County to Wuyuan County, recorded in Shanglin County records.
b_shukun.etymology_analysis: Shukun (述昆) is a historical township name in the Shanglin–Wuming area of central Guangxi, first attested in 1371 CE and likely representing a sinicized Zhuang/Tai-Kadai toponym.

b_gongrao.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b, compiled 1060 CE) as Gongraozhou (功饶州), a jimi prefecture under Yongzhou Dudufu, with no specific establishment year recorded.
b_gongrao.etymology_analysis: Gongrao (功饶, 'Meritorious and Bountiful') is an auspicious Chinese name for a jimi prefecture under Yongzhou Dudufu in the Guangxi–Vietnam borderlands, attested only in the Song-compiled Xin Tangshu.

b_wande.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b, compiled 1060 CE) as Wandezhou (万德州), an undated jimi prefecture under Yongzhou Dudufu (邕州都督府, which itself was established in 632 CE), with no specific establishment year recorded for Wandezhou itself.
b_wande.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Sino-administrative name Wande (万德, 'myriad virtues') given to an undated jimi (loose-rein) prefecture under Yongzhou Dudufu listed in the Song-compiled Xin Tangshu (Vol. 43b) in the Guangxi–Vietnam borderlands; later subordinated to Hengshan Stockade in the Song dynasty and renamed Guide Prefecture.

b_dujiu.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty Kaiyuan era (713–741 CE), when Tianzhou (田州) was established with its seat at Dujiu County (都救县), recorded in the New Book of Tang (Xin Tangshu).

morphemes.translation: rescue, relieve (phonetic rendering of local Tai-Zhuang toponym)

b_dujiu.etymology_analysis: Administrative seat of Tang dynasty Tianzhou (田州), established during the Kaiyuan era (713–741 CE) in modern southeastern Tianyang County, Guangxi. The Chinese characters 都救 (Dujiu) likely transcribe an indigenous Zhuang-Tai toponym.

b_hengshan_1.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty Wude 5 (622 CE), when Hengshan County (横山县) was split from Xuanhua County under Nanjin Prefecture; also a county under Tianzhou (713–741 CE) and Hengshan Commandery (横山郡, 742 CE).
b_hengshan_1.etymology_analysis: Named after a transverse mountain ridge (Hengshan, 横山) in western Guangxi. Attested as Hengshan County in 622 CE and again under Tianzhou in the Kaiyuan era (713–741 CE), with Tianzhou briefly renamed Hengshan Commandery in 742 CE.

b_guiping.first_mention_attestation: Southern Liang dynasty (502–557 CE), when Guiping County (桂平县) was first established in southeastern Guangxi.
b_guiping.etymology_analysis: Established as Guiping County during the Southern Liang dynasty (502–557 CE) at the confluence of the Qian and Yu rivers in Guangxi, combining 'cassia/laurel' (桂, emblematic of Guangxi/Guilin) with 'level plain' (平).

b_dabin.first_mention_attestation: Sui dynasty Daye era (605–618 CE), recorded as Dabin County (大宾县) under Yongping Commandery in the Book of Sui (Suishu Dilizhi); later subordinated to Yanzhou/Xunzhou in 629 CE.
b_dabin.etymology_analysis: Historical county name Dabin (大宾, 'great guest/tributary') located northeast of Guiping in Guangxi, attested in the Sui dynasty (Daye era, 605–618 CE) and incorporated into Tang dynasty Xunzhou/Yanzhou in 629 CE.

b_yulin_1.first_mention_attestation: Western Han dynasty Yuanding 6 (111 BCE), when Han Wudi conquered Nanyue and renamed Qin Guilin Commandery to Yulin Commandery (郁林郡).
b_yulin_1.etymology_analysis: Established in 111 BCE as Yulin Commandery (鬱林郡/郁林郡, 'lush forest'), replacing the Qin dynasty Guilin Commandery; later also used as the name of Yulin County (606 CE) and Yulin Prefecture in Guangxi.

b_xuanhua.first_mention_attestation: Sui dynasty Kaihuang 18 (598 CE), when Jinxing County was renamed Xuanhua County (宣化县) under Yulin Commandery.
b_xuanhua.etymology_analysis: Sino-imperial administrative name Xuanhua (宣化, 'proclaiming civilizing transformation'), bestowed in 598 CE when Sui renamed Eastern Jin Jinxing County; it served as the seat of Tang Yongzhou and modern Nanning.

b_ruhe.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty Wude 5 (622 CE), when Ruhe County (如和县) was split from Nanbin and Anjing counties under Qinzhou; transferred to Yongzhou in 708 CE.
b_ruhe.etymology_analysis: Tang dynasty county established in 622 CE in southern Guangxi near the Vietnamese border, transferred to Yongzhou in 708 CE. Note that the repo calque 'Tathātā Buddhist suchness' for 如 is over-interpreted; in Tang frontier county names 如和 is an auspicious administrative compound or local transcription.

b_wuyaun_1.first_mention_attestation: Sui dynasty Kaihuang 1 (581 CE), when Wuyuan County (武缘县) was established under Yuanzhou (later under Tang Yongzhou in 622 CE).
b_wuyaun_1.etymology_analysis: Predecessor of modern Wuming District (武鸣区) in Nanning, Guangxi. Established in 581 CE as Wuyuan County (武缘县, 'martial frontier') and renamed Wuming in 1912 CE.

b_langning.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty Wude 5 (622 CE), when Langning County (朗宁县) was split from Xuanhua County under Nanjin Prefecture (renamed Yongzhou in 632 CE).
b_langning.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Tang administrative name Langning (朗宁, 'bright tranquility'), established as a county in 622 CE and also used as the commandery name of Yongzhou (Langning Commandery, 742–758 CE).

b_binh_nguyen.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty Kaicheng 4 (839 CE), recorded in Xin Tangshu Vol. 43b (Lingnan Circuit · Annam Protectorate jimi prefectures) as Pingyuan Prefecture / Châu Bình Nguyên (平原州), split from Pingyuanguan of Dujinzhou (and later attested in Lý dynasty 1015 CE in Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư).
b_binh_nguyen.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese administrative name Bình Nguyên (平原 / 平源, 'level/pacified plain'), established in 839 CE as Tang Pingyuan Prefecture (平原州) under the Annam Protectorate and continued under the Lý dynasty (1015 CE) for the Hà Giang / Tuyên Quang frontier. Note that the repo's hanzi '原平' reverses the order Bình Nguyên.

b_vi_long.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty Thuận Thiên 4 (1013 CE), recorded in Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư as Châu Vị Long (渭龍州) in modern Chiêm Hóa, Tuyên Quang.
b_vi_long.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese frontier prefecture name Châu Vị Long (渭隆/渭龍), attested in the early 11th century (1013 CE) under the Lý dynasty in Tuyên Quang; later renamed Châu Đại Man under the Ming and Châu Chiêm Hóa under the Nguyễn.

b_thuong_nguyen.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty Thiên Phù Duệ Vũ 8 (1127 CE), when Châu Thượng Nguyên (上源州) is attested as part of Phủ Phú Lương governed by Dương Tự Minh.
b_thuong_nguyen.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese name Thượng Nguyên (上源, 'upper headwaters'), attested in the 12th century (1127 CE) as a northern upland châu within Phú Lương Prefecture (modern Bắc Kạn / Thái Nguyên area).

b_quang_nguyen.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty Thông Thụy 3 (1036 CE), attested as Châu Quảng Nguyên (廣源州) in modern Cao Bằng during the Nùng Tồn Phúc and Nùng Trí Cao conflicts.
b_quang_nguyen.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese name Quảng Nguyên (廣源/广源, 'broad headwaters'), an 11th-century frontier polity in Cao Bằng famous as the power base of the Nùng clan (Nùng Tồn Phúc and Nùng Trí Cao) and contested between Đại Việt and Song China.

b_nung.first_mention_attestation: 11th century CE (1038–1053 CE), attested in Đại Việt and Song chronicles via the Nùng chieftains (Nùng Tồn Phúc, Nùng Trí Cao) of Quảng Nguyên Châu.
b_nung.etymology_analysis: Represents the Nùng (儂) Tai-Kadai ethnic group/chieftaincy of northeastern Vietnam (Cao Bằng–Lạng Sơn), prominent in 11th-century sources (Nùng Trí Cao). Note that the repo's hanzi '容' (Róng/Dung) is an erroneous character substitution for 儂 (Nùng).

b_hai_dong.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty Đại Định 10 (1149 CE), when foreign merchants entered Hải Đông (海東, modern Quảng Ninh) to trade at Vân Đồn; formally elevated to Lộ Hải Đông in 1242 CE under Trần Thái Tông.
b_hai_dong.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese directional coastal name Hải Đông (海東, 'east of the sea' / 'eastern sea'), applied to the Quảng Ninh–Hải Dương coastal region under the Lý (12th century) and Trần (1242 CE) dynasties.

historical_names.name: Luc Chau
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu Vol. 43a (established as Yushan in 622 CE, renamed Luzhou / Lục Châu in 675 CE)
historical_names.notes: Tang-era Lục Châu (陸州, originally Yushan 622 CE, renamed Luzhou 675 CE) preceded Lý-era Hải Đông (1149 CE) in the Quảng Ninh coastal region.

historical_names.name: Luzhou
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu Vol. 43a (established as Yushan in 622 CE, renamed Luzhou / Lục Châu in 675 CE)
historical_names.notes: Tang-era Lục Châu (陸州, originally Yushan 622 CE, renamed Luzhou 675 CE) preceded Lý-era Hải Đông (1149 CE) in the Quảng Ninh coastal region.

historical_names.name: Yushan
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu Vol. 43a (established as Yushan in 622 CE, renamed Luzhou / Lục Châu in 675 CE)
historical_names.notes: Tang-era Lục Châu (陸州, originally Yushan 622 CE, renamed Luzhou 675 CE) preceded Lý-era Hải Đông (1149 CE) in the Quảng Ninh coastal region.

b_lan_song.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; appears to be an artificial or garbled game-map barony name in Hải Đông (Quảng Ninh) with no pre-867 CE or standard historical attestation.
b_lan_song.etymology_analysis: Unattested historical toponym; the repo renders the key 'b_lan_song' via the Chinese characters 兰双 ('orchid + twin'), likely as a phonetic/calque placeholder rather than a documented Vietnamese settlement.

b_van_asia.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty Đại Định 10 (1149 CE), when Emperor Lý Anh Tông established the maritime trading port of Vân Đồn (雲屯) in Hải Đông (Quảng Ninh).
b_van_asia.etymology_analysis: Corresponds to Vân (Vân Đồn, 雲屯) in Hải Đông, Đại Việt's premier medieval maritime port founded in 1149 CE (with '_asia' added in the game key for disambiguation). Note that the repo's hanzi '范' (Phạm/Fàn) is a character mismatch.

b_lam_tay.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty (1010–1225 CE), when the Điện Biên / northwestern upland region was organized as Châu Lâm Tây (林西州).
b_lam_tay.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese directional name Lâm Tây (林西, 'western forests'), attested under the Lý dynasty (11th–12th century CE) as an upland châu encompassing parts of northwestern Vietnam (Điện Biên).

b_tam_giang.first_mention_attestation: Trần dynasty (1285 CE, Mongol-Đại Việt wars at Bạch Hạc–Tam Giang; later Phủ Tam Giang), located at the confluence of the Red, Lô, and Đà rivers in Phú Thọ.
b_tam_giang.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese name Tam Giang (三江, 'three rivers'), referring to the confluence of the Hồng (Red), Lô, and Đà rivers at Bạch Hạc (Việt Trì, Phú Thọ); prominent as a Trần dynasty military base (1285 CE) and Ming-era prefecture.

historical_names.name: Phong Chau
historical_names.source: Tang dynasty Wude 4 (621 CE) establishment of Phong Châu (峰州) and Bạch Hạc County (白鶴縣) at the same river confluence.
historical_names.notes: Tang-era Phong Châu / Bạch Hạc occupied the exact three-river confluence later known as Tam Giang.

historical_names.name: Bach Hac
historical_names.source: Tang dynasty Wude 4 (621 CE) establishment of Phong Châu (峰州) and Bạch Hạc County (白鶴縣) at the same river confluence.
historical_names.notes: Tang-era Phong Châu / Bạch Hạc occupied the exact three-river confluence later known as Tam Giang.

b_chau_phong.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty Wude 4 (621 CE), when Phong Châu (峰州) was established in modern Phú Thọ; also traditionally remembered as the ancient capital of Văn Lang.
b_chau_phong.etymology_analysis: Historical Sino-Vietnamese prefecture Phong Châu (峰州, 'peak prefecture'), established in 621 CE under the Tang dynasty in modern Phú Thọ. The barony key 'b_chau_phong' and repo hanzi '州峰' reverse the standard order Phong Châu (峰州).

b_ha_giang.first_mention_attestation: Nguyễn dynasty Thiệu Trị 2 (1842 CE), when the northern Tuyên Quang frontier was divided into three jurisdictions (hạt): Hà Giang, Bắc Quang, and Tuyên Quang.
b_ha_giang.etymology_analysis: Modern northernmost Vietnamese province name Hà Giang (河江), formally established as an administrative division in 1842 CE (and a province in 1891 CE), evolving from the earlier settlement name Hà Dương (河楊).

b_quoc_oai.first_mention_attestation: Trần dynasty (1225–1400 CE), when the region west of Thăng Long (modern western Hanoi / Sơn Tây) was organized as Lộ Quốc Oai (國威路).
b_quoc_oai.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese administrative name Quốc Oai (國威, 'majesty of the state'), attested as a major circuit (lộ) under the Trần dynasty (13th–14th century CE) west of Hanoi; briefly renamed Uy Man during Ming occupation (1407 CE).

b_hoang_giang.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty (11th–12th century CE) as Lộ Đại Hoàng Giang, and Trần dynasty (13th–14th century CE) as Lộ Hoàng Giang (黃江路) along the lower Red River in Nam Định/Hà Nam.

natural_proper_name.name: Hoang Giang (Yellow River / lower Red River)

b_hoang_giang.etymology_analysis: Named after the Hoàng Giang ('Yellow River', a historical name for the silt-laden lower Red River / Châu Giang section in Hà Nam–Nam Định), attested as Lộ Đại Hoàng Giang in the Lý dynasty and Lộ Hoàng Giang in the Trần dynasty.

b_son_la.first_mention_attestation: French colonial administration in 1895 CE, when Vạn Bú Province was renamed Sơn La Province (tỉnh Sơn La), adapting the local Tai name Mường La.

morphemes.translation: La (from Tai Mường La, phonetic rendering of indigenous toponym)

b_son_la.etymology_analysis: Modern northwestern Vietnamese province name Sơn La (山羅), coined in 1895 CE by combining Sino-Vietnamese Sơn ('mountain') with La from the indigenous Tai polity name Mường La.

b_muong_lay.first_mention_attestation: Lê dynasty (1435 CE), recorded in Nguyễn Trãi's Dư địa chí as Châu Lai (萊州), transcribing the Tai polity name Mường Lay (believed to have emerged in the 10th century).
b_muong_lay.etymology_analysis: Indigenous White Tai polity name Mường Lay (Sino-Vietnamese Châu Lai 萊州, modern Lai Châu / Mường Lay), attested in Vietnamese written geography from 1435 CE. Note that the repo's hanzi '芒莱' is a phonetic transcription of Mường Lay rather than its classical Sino-Vietnamese form.

b_nam_dinh.first_mention_attestation: Nguyễn dynasty Minh Mạng 3 (1822 CE), when Nam Định (南定) and Ninh Bình (寧平) were established as administrative names (Ninh Bình as a province in 1829–1831 CE).
b_nam_dinh.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Nguyễn-era name Ninh Bình (寧平, 'tranquil and pacified') created in 1822–1829 CE under Emperor Minh Mạng (while the barony key 'b_nam_dinh' reflects the neighboring 1822 CE name Nam Định).

historical_names.name: Truong Chau
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu Vol. 43a (Tang Trường Châu / 長州, established c. 679 CE)
historical_names.notes: The Tang-era Trường Châu (長州, c. 679 CE) administrative region encompassed the Ninh Bình / Hoa Lư area prior to Trường Yên (1010 CE) and Ninh Bình (1822 CE).

historical_names.name: Changzhou
historical_names.source: Xin Tangshu Vol. 43a (Tang Trường Châu / 長州, established c. 679 CE)
historical_names.notes: The Tang-era Trường Châu (長州, c. 679 CE) administrative region encompassed the Ninh Bình / Hoa Lư area prior to Trường Yên (1010 CE) and Ninh Bình (1822 CE).

b_thanh_hoa.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty Thiên Thành 2 (1029 CE), when Emperor Lý Thái Tông renamed Ái Châu to Thanh Hóa Prefecture (清化府).
b_thanh_hoa.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese administrative name Thanh Hóa (清化, 'pure civilizing transformation'), coined in 1029 CE under Lý Thái Tông to replace the older Tang-era name Ái Châu.

historical_names.name: Cuu Chan
historical_names.source: Western Han dynasty Yuanding 6 (111 BCE) establishment of Cửu Chân Commandery (九真郡); renamed Ái Châu (愛州) by the Liang dynasty in 523 CE.
historical_names.notes: Known as Cửu Chân from 111 BCE and Ái Châu from 523 CE through the Tang dynasty until 1029 CE.

historical_names.name: Ai Chau
historical_names.source: Western Han dynasty Yuanding 6 (111 BCE) establishment of Cửu Chân Commandery (九真郡); renamed Ái Châu (愛州) by the Liang dynasty in 523 CE.
historical_names.notes: Known as Cửu Chân from 111 BCE and Ái Châu from 523 CE through the Tang dynasty until 1029 CE.

b_lam_son.first_mention_attestation: Early 15th century (1418 CE), during Lê Lợi's Lam Sơn uprising against Ming rule in Thanh Hóa (renamed Lam Kinh / Tây Kinh in 1430 CE).
b_lam_son.etymology_analysis: Named after the Lam Sơn ('indigo mountain') area in Thọ Xuân, Thanh Hóa, famous as the ancestral home of Lê Lợi and the launching site of the 1418 CE Lam Sơn uprising.

b_truong_yen.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty Thuận Thiên 1 (1010 CE), when Hoa Lư was renamed Phủ Trường An (長安府, later pronounced Trường Yên) after the capital moved to Thăng Long.
b_truong_yen.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese name Trường Yên (from Trường An 長安, 'enduring peace'), bestowed on the former Đinh–Early Lê capital of Hoa Lư in 1010 CE in emulation of Han Chang'an (with An pronounced Yên due to naming taboo).
