b_nghe_an.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty Thiên Thành 3 (1030 CE), when Emperor Lý Thái Tông renamed Hoan Châu to Nghệ An Châu (乂安州).
b_nghe_an.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese auspicious name Nghệ An (乂安, 'governed and pacified'), introduced in 1030 CE by Lý Thái Tông to replace the Tang-era name Hoan Châu.

historical_names.name: Hoan Chau
historical_names.source: Tang dynasty Zhenguan 1 (627 CE), when Đức Châu was renamed Hoan Châu (歡州); earlier Cửu Đức (九德) in the Six Dynasties.
historical_names.notes: Known as Hoan Châu throughout the Tang dynasty until renamed Nghệ An in 1030 CE.

historical_names.name: Cuu Duc
historical_names.source: Tang dynasty Zhenguan 1 (627 CE), when Đức Châu was renamed Hoan Châu (歡州); earlier Cửu Đức (九德) in the Six Dynasties.
historical_names.notes: Known as Hoan Châu throughout the Tang dynasty until renamed Nghệ An in 1030 CE.

b_dien_chau.first_mention_attestation: Tang dynasty Zhenguan 1 (627 CE), when former Hoan Châu was renamed Diễn Châu (演州).
b_dien_chau.etymology_analysis: Tang dynasty prefecture Diễn Châu (演州, 'wide-flowing prefecture'), established in 627 CE in northern Nghệ An and continuously attested through the Lý, Trần, and Lê dynasties.

b_nghe_an_2.first_mention_attestation: Nguyễn dynasty Minh Mạng 12 (1831 CE), when Hà Tĩnh Province (河靜省) was established.
b_nghe_an_2.etymology_analysis: Modern provincial name Hà Tĩnh (河靜), coined in 1831 CE under Emperor Minh Mạng by combining characters from constituent prefectures when dividing Nghệ An into Nghệ An and Hà Tĩnh.

historical_names.name: Hoan Chau
historical_names.source: Tang dynasty Zhenguan 1 (627 CE) Hoan Châu (歡州), encompassing modern Nghệ An and Hà Tĩnh.
historical_names.notes: Part of Cửu Đức and Tang-era Hoan Châu prior to the 1831 CE creation of Hà Tĩnh.

historical_names.name: Cuu Duc
historical_names.source: Tang dynasty Zhenguan 1 (627 CE) Hoan Châu (歡州), encompassing modern Nghệ An and Hà Tĩnh.
historical_names.notes: Part of Cửu Đức and Tang-era Hoan Châu prior to the 1831 CE creation of Hà Tĩnh.

b_tra_lan.first_mention_attestation: Early 15th century (1424 CE), when Lê Lợi's Lam Sơn forces besieged Trà Lân Citadel (Thành Trà Lân / Trà Long) in western Nghệ An.

morphemes.translation: tea (phonetic rendering of local Tai/Austroasiatic toponym)

b_tra_lan.etymology_analysis: Historical frontier prefecture Phủ Trà Lân in western Nghệ An (modern Con Cuông), attested in 1424 CE during the Lam Sơn uprising and immortalized in Nguyễn Trãi's Bình Ngô đại cáo.

b_sam_nuea.first_mention_attestation: Early 20th century (1903 CE), when deposed Phrae ruler Phiriya Thepphawong took refuge in Xam Neua (Houaphanh Province, Laos); the Tai/Lao toponym itself predates colonial records.
b_sam_nuea.etymology_analysis: Lao/Tai toponym Xam Neua (Sam Nuea, Vietnamese Sầm Nưa), literally 'northern swamp'. Note that the repo's hanzi '桑怒' is a purely phonetic Chinese transcription (which the repo mistakenly calqued as 'mulberry + rage').

b_hua_muong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written historical sources by 867 CE; modern district in Houaphanh Province, northeastern Laos.
b_hua_muong.etymology_analysis: Lao/Tai toponym Hua Muong ('head/upper district') in Houaphanh Province, Laos. The repo's hanzi '华芒' is a phonetic transcription of Hua Muong rather than a semantic compound.

b_long_hung.first_mention_attestation: Trần dynasty (1225–1258 CE under Trần Thái Tông), when Long Hưng Prefecture/Circuit (龍興府/路) was established in modern Hưng Hà, Thái Bình.
b_long_hung.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Trần dynasty administrative name Long Hưng (龍興, 'exalted rise'), bestowed in the 13th century on the ancestral homeland of the Trần clan in the Red River Delta.

b_kien_xuong.first_mention_attestation: Trần dynasty (1225–1258 CE under Trần Thái Tông), when Phủ Kiến Xương (建昌府) was established in modern Thái Bình Province.
b_kien_xuong.etymology_analysis: Auspicious Sino-Vietnamese administrative name Kiến Xương (建昌, 'establishing prosperity'), first attested as a Trần dynasty prefecture/circuit in the 13th century CE.

b_tan_hung.first_mention_attestation: Trần dynasty (13th century CE), when Phủ lộ Tân Hưng (新興府路) was established in the Hưng Yên–Thái Bình delta region.
b_tan_hung.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese administrative name Tân Hưng (新興, 'newly rising/prospering'), created under the Trần dynasty in the 13th century CE (renamed Tân An during the 1407 CE Ming occupation).

b_thang_long.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty Thuận Thiên 1 (1010 CE), when Emperor Lý Thái Tổ issued the Edict on the Transfer of the Capital, moving from Hoa Lư to Đại La Citadel and renaming it Thăng Long (昇龍).
b_thang_long.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese imperial capital name Thăng Long (昇龍, 'ascending dragon'), bestowed by Lý Thái Tổ in 1010 CE after reportedly seeing a golden dragon rise above the Red River at Đại La.

historical_names.name: Tong Binh
historical_names.source: Liu Song dynasty (454 CE) establishment of Tống Bình (宋平); later fortified as Đại La Citadel (大羅城) in 767 CE and 866 CE under the Tang Protectorate of Annam.
historical_names.notes: Known as Tống Bình from 454 CE and Đại La from 767 CE until renamed Thăng Long in 1010 CE.

historical_names.name: Dai La
historical_names.source: Liu Song dynasty (454 CE) establishment of Tống Bình (宋平); later fortified as Đại La Citadel (大羅城) in 767 CE and 866 CE under the Tang Protectorate of Annam.
historical_names.notes: Known as Tống Bình from 454 CE and Đại La from 767 CE until renamed Thăng Long in 1010 CE.

b_ha_bac.first_mention_attestation: 27 October 1962 CE, when the National Assembly of North Vietnam merged Bắc Ninh and Bắc Giang provinces into Hà Bắc Province (tỉnh Hà Bắc, dissolved in 1996).
b_ha_bac.etymology_analysis: Modern 20th-century Vietnamese provincial name Hà Bắc (河北, 'north of the [Red] River'), created in 1962 CE by merging Bắc Ninh and Bắc Giang.

historical_names.name: Long Bien
historical_names.source: Western Han dynasty (111 BCE / 2 CE Hanshu Dilizhi) Long Biên (龍編); later Tang-era Vũ Ninh (武寧).
historical_names.notes: The Bắc Ninh–Bắc Giang region north of the Red River was historically the seat of Han-Tang Long Biên and Vũ Ninh.

historical_names.name: Vu Ninh
historical_names.source: Western Han dynasty (111 BCE / 2 CE Hanshu Dilizhi) Long Biên (龍編); later Tang-era Vũ Ninh (武寧).
historical_names.notes: The Bắc Ninh–Bắc Giang region north of the Red River was historically the seat of Han-Tang Long Biên and Vũ Ninh.

b_phu_luong.first_mention_attestation: Lý dynasty Thiên Phù Duệ Vũ 8 (1127 CE), when Dương Tự Minh was appointed to govern Phủ Phú Lương (富良府) covering modern Thái Nguyên, Bắc Kạn, and Cao Bằng.
b_phu_luong.etymology_analysis: Sino-Vietnamese auspicious prefecture name Phủ Phú Lương (富良府, 'wealthy and good'), first attested in the Lý dynasty (early 12th century CE, 1127 CE) in Thái Nguyên.
